findings.title: Core tautology: 'stable top-K' validates the default, not correctness
findings.claim: The benchmark claims to validate the default window choice (full history) by measuring Jaccard overlap and recency contamination. But it only measures whether results are *stable across different windows*, not whether the results are *correct* for actual refactoring prioritization.
findings.evidence: The script explicitly states: 'There's no labelled ground truth on the bench' and instead measures two proxies: (1) Jaccard overlap between window-specific top-K sets, and (2) fraction of full-history top-K not in 12-month top-K. Neither of these validates whether users should actually refactor the files on the hotspots list. The median J(full, 12mo)=0.60 simply means that 60% of modules overlap when comparing two windows — it does NOT validate that these modules are real refactoring opportunities.
findings.impact: The default window choice (full history) may be suboptimal or even wrong for active projects. A user gets a 'hotspots' ranking that claims to prioritize refactoring work, but lacks any validation that the ranking serves the user's actual goal (reducing technical debt, improving testability, etc.). An alternative hypothesis — that recent-churn hotspots (12mo or 6mo) are more actionable — cannot be ruled out.
findings.suggested_action: Either: (a) acknowledge in the docstring that stability is orthogonal to correctness, and add a caveat that users should compare full-history hotspots against their own ground truth before trusting the ranking; or (b) run a small validation study where developers are asked to refactor top-5 hotspots from each window (full, 12mo, 6mo) and measure which produces better outcomes (fewer new hotspots, faster refactoring, better test coverage gains, etc.). Without this, the default is an educated guess, not evidence-based.
findings.verifier_reasoning: The finding correctly identifies that the benchmark measures *stability* (whether window choice affects the top-K ranking) rather than *correctness* (whether those files should actually be refactored). The bench script is explicitly honest about this (lines 4-5: "There's no labelled ground truth on the bench"). However, the severity claim of "blocker tautology" overstates the actual problem. The codebase does distinguish between the benchmark's goal (justifying full history as a practical default) and correctness claims. In hotspots.py lines 24-31, the rationale is engineering-sound: full history is the only window that produces stable top-K on low-activity projects, with ~25% median recency contamination acknowledged as a tradeoff. RESEARCH_METRICS.md §8 correctly frames hotspots as "very actionable" and grounded in Tornhill (2015) but does not claim the bench validates *correctness*. The real issue is that user-facing documentation (SIXTY_SECOND_TOUR: "The top of the list is where refactoring effort pays back the most") lacks caveats about what "pays back" means and lacks guidance to validate against ground truth. This is a communication/documentation gap, not a logical tautology in the design itself.
findings.ticket_notes: RECLASSIFIED from blocker to minor. The bench itself is honestly scoped: it validates window choice stability, not correctness. The real gap is user-facing clarity. Suggested fixes: (1) In CLI help/SIXTY_SECOND_TOUR, add a caveat that "hotspots" is a heuristic based on CC × churn (Tornhill 2015) and users should validate against their refactoring outcomes; (2) In docstrings, elevate the "diagnostic" label so it reaches the user (not just code comments); (3) Optionally, note that recent-churn hotspots (`--since 12.months`) may be more actionable for active projects. Not a correctness bug - the design is defensible - but needs documentation clarity to set proper expectations.

findings.title: Stale_frac is a set-difference metric, not a churn measurement
findings.claim: The metric `stale_full_frac = |full_top_20 - 12mo_top_K| / |full_top_20|` is presented as measuring 'recency contamination' (complex-but-dead files). But it only measures set difference, not actual churn. A module can be absent from 12mo top-K for three reasons: (1) it's dead (zero recent churn), (2) it was fixed/refactored so recent churn is zero by design, (3) recent churn is non-zero but low enough that other modules ranked higher.
findings.evidence: The metric computes set operations on module names, not churn values. The code at hotspots.py:26-31 states: 'A complex but stable file is load-bearing but tolerable' — this is interpretation (2), where zero recent churn is the GOAL, not a failure mode. Yet stale_frac treats it as bad. The bench never validates the actual churn of modules in (full_top_20 - 12mo_top_K) to distinguish which case applies.
findings.impact: The 'stale_frac' metric could be misleading users. A high stale_frac (0.25 median) might mean: (a) 25% of hotspots are dead code (bad), (b) 25% of hotspots are well-engineered and stable (good), or (c) a mix. Without looking at actual churn values, users cannot tell.
findings.suggested_action: Rename the metric to avoid the 'stale' framing, or compute it correctly by checking the actual git churn of modules in the difference set. Add a validation step: for projects where stale_frac > 0.5, inspect the actual 12mo churn of those modules and report whether they are truly zero-churn (dead) or just lower-churn (stable but active).
findings.verifier_reasoning: The bench code at hotspots_sweep.py:156-158 computes `stale_full_frac = len(full_mods - twelve) / len(full_mods)` which is pure set difference on module names. The code extracts only module names from hotspot results (line 142-144) and discards all churn values. The docstring at lines 12-14 claims the metric measures "fraction of full-history top-K modules whose 12-month churn is zero" but the implementation never validates actual 12-month churn values. A module absent from the 12-month top-K can have three causes: (1) zero 12-month churn (dead), (2) low but non-zero churn (stable/well-engineered), or (3) non-zero churn but ranked outside top-20. The metric conflates all three without distinguishing them. The interpretation is further contradicted by hotspots.py:5-6 which states "complex but stable file is load-bearing but tolerable" (implying low churn is acceptable/good) yet the metric treats absence from 12mo top-K as "recency contamination" (bad). The design does acknowledge this tradeoff explicitly in hotspots.py:24-31, documenting ~25% median "recency contamination" as the cost of using full history over 12-month windows on low-activity projects.
findings.ticket_notes: The metric name and documentation are misleading. Either: (1) Rename to avoid "stale" framing (e.g., `not_in_12mo_frac` or `window_drift_frac`) to reflect what it actually measures (set difference), or (2) Implement the claimed metric by extracting actual 12-month churn values from the hotspot results and checking which modules in (full_mods - twelve) have zero 12-month churn vs. non-zero. The bench has access to full churn data from the Hotspot objects but discards it. A validation step should be added: for projects where stale_frac > 0.5, sample the actual 12mo churn of modules in the difference set and report the breakdown (zero-churn vs. lower-churn). Example problematic case: mkdocs at 1.00 stale_frac (line 31) - the single 12mo hotspot means 100% of the full top-20 are "stale", but this could mean they're all dead or all just ranked #21-40 with non-zero churn. Documentation should clarify the three-case ambiguity and the contradiction with hotspots.py's "complex but stable = good" principle.

findings.title: Low-activity projects confound the 'stability' metric
findings.location: bench/hotspots_results.md (rows for httpx, mkdocs, click, etc.)
findings.claim: Projects with incomplete 12mo result sets (e.g., httpx: 12mo=10, mkdocs: 12mo=1) automatically produce low Jaccard values and high stale_frac. The bench does not distinguish between (a) 'window choice is genuinely important because the project is mixed-activity' and (b) 'low J and high stale_frac are artifacts of project inactivity.'
findings.evidence: Active projects (|12mo|=20, i.e., have >=20 hotspots in recent window): median J(full,12mo)=0.60, median stale_frac=0.25. Inactive projects (|12mo|<20): median J(full,12mo)=0.35, median stale_frac=0.60. The inactivity level is a strong confound. mkdocs (|12mo|=1) has J=0.00 and stale=1.00 — which is just mathematical consequence of having one file in 12mo, not evidence of window-choice importance.
findings.impact: The global medians (J=0.600, stale=0.250) are misleading because they aggregate over projects with vastly different activity levels, without stratification. A user cannot tell: 'does full-history work well across all projects?' vs. 'does it only work well on actively-developed projects?'
findings.suggested_action: Stratify results by project activity: show J and stale_frac separately for active (|12mo|=20) vs. inactive (|12mo|<20) projects. Explain that low J and high stale_frac on inactive projects may reflect inactivity, not window-choice failure. Consider excluding projects with |12mo|<20 from the median calculations, or report both medians (all projects vs. active-only).
findings.verifier_reasoning: I verified the finding by examining: (1) the raw data in bench/hotspots_results.md showing all 27 projects with their |12mo| sizes, J(full,12mo), and stale_frac values; (2) the benchmark script (hotspots_sweep.py) which computes global medians without stratification; (3) mathematical verification that mkdocs (|12mo|=1) must have J=0.0 and stale=1.0 as a mathematical consequence, not evidence of window-choice failure; (4) the codebase documentation (LEARNINGS.md) which explicitly states "low-activity codebases (mkdocs collapses to 1 hotspot at 12 months, httpx to 10) make a 12-month default unworkable - the metric would vanish on stable codebases." All quantitative claims in the finding match the actual data: active projects (n=23, |12mo|=20) have median J=0.60 and stale=0.25; inactive projects (n=4, |12mo|<20) have median J=0.35 and stale=0.60. The Pearson correlation is strong: r(|12mo| vs J)=0.696, r(|12mo| vs stale)=-0.859, confirming a confound. The core issue is real: the benchmark report aggregates medians without stratification, obscuring whether results hold across all projects or only active ones.
findings.ticket_notes: The bench/hotspots_results.md report should be updated to: (1) Stratify J(full,12mo) and stale_frac by activity level (active: |12mo|=20 vs inactive: |12mo|<20), showing both median sets; (2) Add a footnote explaining that inactive projects with low |12mo| produce mathematically-driven low J and high stale_frac due to small sample size, not window-choice failure; (3) Clarify whether the global medians (J=0.600, stale=0.250) are meant to apply to all projects or only active ones. NOTE: The underlying issue is already acknowledged in LEARNINGS.md (lines 168-169) and hotspots.py docstring (lines 24-31), so the ticket is a documentation/presentation fix to the bench report, not a hidden architectural problem. The code correctly defaults to full history and documents the recency-contamination tradeoff. Suggest: update hotspots_results.md with a "Activity level analysis" section showing the stratified medians and explaining the confound, similar to how the text was explained in LEARNINGS.md.

findings.title: Archy self-entry (v0.22.0) is a poisoned control with J=1.00
findings.claim: Including archy itself (pinned to a release tag v0.22.0) in the benchmark inflates the correlation metrics. The entry shows perfect overlap (J=1.00) and zero stale fraction. This is not evidence that 'full history is a good default' — it's evidence that 'a frozen codebase has stable hotspots.'
findings.evidence: The comment in projects.yaml states: 'Pin to a release tag, not HEAD: every merged commit was silently shifting archy's row in the score table...' This is a snapshot, not a living project. Of course the hotspots are identical across windows when the code was released months ago. The median J=0.600 includes this inflating datapoint.
findings.impact: The benchmark's median metrics are biased upward by one datapoint that is not representative of real active projects. An external observer reading the results cannot tell that one of 27 projects is a frozen snapshot.
findings.suggested_action: Either (a) exclude archy from the median calculation and report it separately as 'dogfooding (pinned snapshot),' or (b) compute archy's hotspots at *two different points in time* (e.g., two release tags, or HEAD at two different months) and measure the cross-time J to validate temporal stability rather than within-snapshot stability.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
The finding is technically correct on all substantive claims:

1. CONFIRMED: Archy at v0.18.0 shows J(full,12mo)=1.00 and stale_full_frac=0.00. Verification: The archy repository was created 2026-05-09, v0.18.0 was tagged 2026-05-15 (6 days later), and hotspots_results.md was captured that same day. When hotspots_sweep.py runs on a pinned 6-day-old tag with --since=12.months and --since=6.months filters, all three windows capture identical commit history (the entire 6-day repo), resulting in identical hotspot sets and perfect Jaccard index.

2. CONFIRMED: This measures "snapshot stability" not "temporal stability". A frozen codebase will trivially produce identical hotspots across time windows, regardless of whether full history is a good default for living projects.

3. CONFIRMED: The comment in projects.yaml (lines 183-186) acknowledges pinning but only addresses the problem of "every merged commit was silently shifting archy's row" — it doesn't address the conceptual issue that a frozen snapshot is not a valid test case for validating temporal window choice.

4. NUMERICAL IMPACT: Removing archy from the 27-project median doesn't change it mathematically (remains 0.60 either way), but this doesn't invalidate the finding's core concern about research-method validity.

5. INTERPRETATION IMPACT: The FUTURE.md documentation (line about "Median Jaccard(full, 12mo) = 0.60 across the bench") draws conclusions about window stability based on this data, but one of the 27 projects doesn't actually measure what the others measure.
findings.ticket_notes:
The finding correctly identifies that archy's benchmark entry uses a fundamentally different measurement than the other 26 projects. The suggested remedies are sound:
- Option (a): Report archy separately as "dogfooding (pinned snapshot)" and exclude from median, with a note that the 0.60 median is across 26 active projects
- Option (b): Measure archy at two different release tags (e.g., v0.18.0 and v0.22.0) to compute cross-release Jaccard as a genuine temporal-stability test

The finding does NOT claim the reported median (0.60) is mathematically wrong — it claims the *interpretation* is compromised because one data point doesn't measure the intended concept. This is a research-methods issue, not a data-integrity issue. The fix should preserve reproducibility of hotspots_results.md (don't change the table) while clarifying the documentation about what was actually measured and whether archy's entry is directly comparable to the other 26.

findings.title: No temporal validation: script doesn't test whether hotspots change across time
findings.location: bench/hotspots_sweep.py (entire script): only measures J across windows at a single point in time
findings.claim: The bench measures J(full, 12mo), J(12mo, 6mo), etc. at a single point in time (2026-05-15). It never measures J(full_may2026, full_march2026) or similar. This means the bench cannot validate whether 'stable across windows at time T' implies 'stable across time' — which is what a user actually cares about.
findings.evidence: The script runs hotspots on each project once, then computes pairwise Jaccard on the windows. There is no loop over multiple time points. A user wants to know: 'if I run `archy hotspots` every month, will the top-K set bounce around?' The bench cannot answer this because it only sampled one month.
findings.impact: The benchmark may give false confidence in the default. A default window that produces consistent results across (full, 12mo, 6mo) at a single point may still produce wildly different results at different points in time — the thing the user actually cares about.
findings.suggested_action: Extend the bench to run at multiple time points (e.g., 2025-11, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-05) and compute temporal Jaccard J(t1_full, t2_full), J(t1_12mo, t2_12mo), etc. This would validate whether the default is temporally stable, not just window-stable.
findings.verifier_reasoning: The bench script measures J(full, 12mo, 6mo) at a single point in time (2026-05-15 per hotspots_results.md line 3). The WINDOWS constant defines window sizes as relative durations ("12.months", "6.months"), not dates, and there is no loop over multiple dates in the main function. The script measures whether different window sizes produce stable top-K sets at one moment in time, not whether the same window produces stable results across multiple time points. The claim is technically accurate: the benchmark does not test temporal stability (month-to-month drift) despite that being a legitimate user concern for recurring metric runs. However, the benchmark's documented purpose (per LEARNINGS.md v0.18.0 section and the commit message) is explicitly window-size stability, not temporal stability - the distinction between "does window width matter" vs "does the metric change over time." The finding correctly identifies a gap but mischaracterizes it as a failure of the stated purpose rather than a gap beyond the stated scope.
findings.ticket_notes: The gap is real and the suggested action (loop over multiple time points like 2025-11, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-05) is valid and actionable. However, clarify in the ticket that the current benchmark validates window-size stability, not temporal stability. The question "will top-K bounce month-to-month?" is genuinely unanswered by the existing bench and is a distinct validation axis from "does window size choice matter?" If temporal stability becomes a design concern, the proposed extension (multiple time-point sweeps with temporal Jaccard) is the right approach.

findings.title: Jaccard is inflated when comparing sets of different sizes due to union denominator
findings.claim: For projects where |12mo| < TOP_K (e.g., httpx with 10 vs. 20), Jaccard conflates two signals: (1) overlap proportion, and (2) result-set incompleteness. When one set is much smaller, the Jaccard can look high due to the smaller set, even if the large set changes a lot.
findings.evidence: Example: if full={A,B,C,...,T} (20 items) and 12mo={A,B,C,D,E} (5 items), then J = 5/(20+5-5) = 5/20 = 0.25 even though the overlap is 100%. This conflates 'both windows agree on top-5' (good) with 'we're missing items in 12mo' (neutral/expected). The metric doesn't distinguish.
findings.impact: Projects with low activity (small 12mo result sets) may report misleading Jaccard values. The metric becomes more about 'did we get enough hotspots?' than 'do the windows agree?'
findings.suggested_action: Consider reporting intersection size and union size separately, not just Jaccard. Or use Jaccard on the *common size* (e.g., J(top_5_full, top_5_12mo)) to make the comparison fair. Document that Jaccard is size-dependent.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
The finding's mathematical claim about Jaccard size-dependency is theoretically correct: when |12mo| < TOP_K, the Jaccard denominator includes both sets fully, so J = |A∩B| / |A∪B| can yield surprisingly low values even with perfect overlap (e.g., 5/(20+5-5) = 0.25). This is real and mathematically sound.

However, the claim of *inflation* (making agreement look better than it is) does not hold in the actual data:
- mkdocs (|12mo|=1): J=0.00 shows complete disagreement, not inflation
- httpx (|12mo|=10): J=0.15 shows low values indicating real disagreement, not inflation
- All 27 projects show set sizes explicitly in the output table

The code already mitigates the theoretical problem through:
1. Explicit reporting of |full|, |12mo|, |6mo| in separate table columns
2. Clear Jaccard formula documentation ("|A intersect B| / |A union B|")
3. A separate stale_full_frac metric that directly captures recency signal
4. LEARNINGS.md acknowledging the window size dependency

The real issue is not inflation but rather *interpretation difficulty*: if read in isolation without set sizes, Jaccard values can be misleading. This is a presentation/documentation concern, not a metric corruption issue. The metric itself is working as designed; it's just size-dependent, which requires context (the set sizes) to interpret correctly—and that context is provided.
findings.ticket_notes:
The finding correctly identifies that Jaccard is size-dependent and smaller result sets require more context to interpret. However, this is a well-understood limitation already documented in LEARNINGS.md and the code already provides the necessary context (explicit set sizes and stale_full_frac metric).

If any action is taken, it should focus on:
1. Clarifying documentation that Jaccard should always be read WITH the set sizes (|full|, |12mo|), not in isolation
2. Emphasizing that stale_full_frac is the primary recency-contamination signal, not Jaccard
3. Consider adding a note in bench/hotspots_results.md explaining that on low-activity projects (|12mo| < TOP_K), Jaccard can look low even with good overlap—refer readers to the set-size columns

The metric itself does not need to change. The benchmark already produces excellent results (median J=0.60 full-vs-12mo, matching the documented finding that "the window genuinely matters"). The issue is one of reader interpretation, not metric design.

findings.title: No sensitivity analysis: TOP_K=20 is arbitrary and not validated
findings.claim: The bench uses TOP_K=20 without justification or sensitivity testing. Some projects produce exactly 20 hotspots (starlette, many others), suggesting either: (a) they genuinely have only 20, or (b) the default is capping at 20. If (b), then results for those projects are artifacts of the choice.
findings.evidence: Most projects in results.md report |full|=20, |12mo|=20, |6mo|=20. This suggests the result sets are being capped at the TOP_K. If the true hotspot count is higher, then Jaccard comparisons are comparing two truncations, not full rankings.
findings.impact: Users may not realize that the top-20 hotspots could change significantly if they run with --top 30 or --top 100. The bench doesn't validate that the window-choice conclusion holds across different K values.
findings.suggested_action: Run a sensitivity analysis: compute J(full, 12mo) for multiple K values (K=5, 10, 20, 50) and show whether the conclusions hold. Document that the default K=20 was chosen empirically or arbitrarily.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I verified the bench finding by examining the code and results:

1. **Code verification**: The bench/hotspots_sweep.py line 99 extracts only `json.loads(res.stdout).get("hotspots", [])`, discarding the "total" field that would reveal the true count. The CLI (cli.py line 1596-1598) returns both "total" (actual count computed) and "hotspots" (capped at --top N), but the bench script ignores "total".

2. **Results table artifact**: The bench results show ALL 27 projects with exactly |full|=20, |12mo|=20, and |6mo|=20 (or fewer). This is suspicious for a distribution across diverse projects.

3. **Actual data verification**: Running `archy hotspots` on cached projects reveals the capping:
   - starlette: computed 63 total hotspots, results show 20
   - rich: computed 154 total hotspots, results show 20
   - httpx: computed 54 total hotspots, results show 20
   - click: computed 20 total hotspots, results show 20 (happens to match)
   - flask: computed 38 total hotspots, results show 20

4. **Sensitivity is real**: Testing different K values on starlette shows Jaccard values change measurably (K=5→0.667, K=20→0.739, K=100→0.714 for J(full,12mo)), confirming that window-choice conclusions depend on the K value chosen.

5. **No sensitivity analysis in codebase**: Searching for "sensitivity", "validate", "justify", "multiple K" in bench files yields no evidence that TOP_K=20 was ever tested against alternative values.

6. **Documentation gap**: LEARNINGS.md thoroughly documents why the full-history window was chosen empirically (25% recency contamination, 0.60 Jaccard median, collapse issues with low-activity projects), but makes NO mention of why TOP_K=20 was chosen. The v0.19.0 section states `top=20` as a parameter default but does not justify it.

7. **Arbitrary appearance**: The choice appears to be arbitrary—neither validated against alternatives nor documented with empirical reasoning, unlike the --since window choice which is well-justified.
findings.ticket_notes:
This is a **CONFIRMED FINDING** with evidence of actual data capping. The bench is valid as-is *for comparing window effects at K=20 specifically*, but the issue ticket should capture:

1. **The bench measures artifact, not ground truth**: All hotspot counts in results.md are capped at TOP_K. To avoid user confusion, the results table should add a clarifying note: "All counts capped at --top 20; see JSON response 'total' field for full counts."

2. **TOP_K=20 lacks empirical justification**: Unlike the --since window choice (which has documented tradeoffs: median Jaccard, stale fraction, low-activity collapse), the K value was never tested. A sensitivity analysis is needed to either (a) validate that conclusions hold across K={5,10,20,50,100}, or (b) document the choice was arbitrary.

3. **Impact on users**: Users may assume "top 20 hotspots" means the top 20 most important files. In reality, for rich (154 true hotspots), they're seeing only the top 13% of the list. The --top parameter is documented as "Maximum hotspots to show" but not why 20 is the default.

4. **Recommended actions**:
   - (Minor fix) Update hotspots_results.md table header or caption to clarify "Shown top-20 (total column in JSON); rerun with --top N to see full ranking"
   - (Investigation) Run sensitivity analysis: sweep hotspots_sweep.py with K=[5,10,20,50,100] and check if median Jaccard / recency findings hold. If findings are robust across K, document this. If not, justify the K=20 choice or raise it.
   - (Documentation) Add to LEARNINGS.md v0.18.0 section: "Defaulting to top-20 was chosen as a practical limit (email/TUI display width); no sensitivity analysis validates this choice against alternatives. Use --top N to retrieve full ranking."

5. **Severity is MAJOR not MINOR** because: (a) the benchmark measures capped truncations, not rankings (both the bench's Jaccard and users' results are artifacts of K), and (b) documentation/docstrings don't disclose this limitation, potentially misleading users about the stability of top-K conclusions.

findings.title: Implicit assumption: 'if windows agree, default is correct' is unvalidated
findings.location: bench/hotspots_sweep.py:8-10 (docstring comment: 'If the window doesn't move the top-K set, the default doesn't matter much')
findings.claim: The script's opening statement assumes that window stability implies the default choice doesn't matter. But this is only true if the goal is 'make a decision that's robust to window choice.' If the goal is 'choose the window that best predicts refactoring outcomes,' then stability is irrelevant — correctness is all that matters.
findings.evidence: The docstring says: 'If the window doesn't move the top-K set, the default doesn't matter much.' This inverts the logic. If the default is full-history and windows DON'T move the set, it could mean: (1) good, any default works, OR (2) bad, we haven't tested the full-history default's correctness. The bench cannot tell.
findings.impact: Users may be misled into thinking that J=0.60 is evidence that the default is good. It only shows window-stability within this one snapshot, not default-correctness.
findings.suggested_action: Reword the opening docstring to clarify: 'This script measures whether different windows produce similar top-K sets. HIGH Jaccard means results are window-stable (less sensitive to recent vs. historical data). However, window-stability does NOT validate that the results are correct — i.e., that users should actually refactor the files on the list. To validate correctness, this script would need ground truth labels or a longitudinal study of refactoring outcomes.'
findings.verifier_reasoning: The docstring at lines 8-10 of /Users/hosanglee/archy/bench/hotspots_sweep.py makes an unvalidated logical assumption: that window stability (measured by Jaccard similarity across --since windows) implies the default window choice (full history) is correct. However, these are distinct concepts. High Jaccard (e.g., 0.82 for starlette) means results are robust to window choice—but this does NOT tell you whether the results are actually correct for real refactoring decisions. The script explicitly acknowledges "There's no labelled ground truth on the bench" (line 4-5), yet the docstring implicitly claims that if windows agree, "the default doesn't matter much"—assuming that agreement equals validity. Validating whether full history is the right default would require ground truth (labeled refactoring outcomes) or longitudinal studies tracking whether developers following the hotspots list actually solve architectural problems. The Jaccard metric alone cannot provide this.
findings.ticket_notes: The docstring conflates two concepts: (1) window-stability (a robustness metric) and (2) default-validity (a correctness claim). The Jaccard measurements in the output (median J(full,12mo) = 0.600) show agreement rates, not correctness validation. The suggested fix is to explicitly clarify in the docstring that high Jaccard means "results are robust to window choice / less sensitive to recent vs. historical data" but that "window-stability does NOT validate that the results are correct — i.e., that users should actually refactor the files on the list." To validate correctness would require ground truth labels (files that developers actually should refactor) or longitudinal outcome tracking. This is documentation clarity, not a behavioral bug, but it could mislead users into misinterpreting benchmark results as evidence that the full-history default is validated when only its robustness has been tested.

findings.title: Cycle.edges field not compared in oracle
findings.claim: The oracle compares only the modules in cycles, not the edges within cycles. A bug that produces a cycle with the correct module set but different CycleEdge entries (different lines metadata) would pass undetected.
findings.evidence: _cycle_keys returns only (frozenset(frozenset(c.modules) for c in cd.added), frozenset(frozenset(c.modules) for c in cd.resolved)), completely ignoring c.edges which contains CycleEdge objects with source, target, and lines fields. The Cycle class (src/archy/cycles.py:17-21) defines both modules and edges, but only modules are compared.
findings.impact: A regression in how cycle edges are computed or reported (e.g., if edge attribution in cycles becomes incorrect) would not be caught by the oracle, even on clean samples. The oracle reports 0 bugs with 100% pass rate, but this may mask edge-level bugs.
findings.suggested_action: Expand _cycle_keys to also compare cycle edges: compare the full set of (source, target) pairs from c.edges, not just the module set. This will catch bugs where cycles have correct module membership but incorrect internal structure.
findings.verifier_reasoning: I analyzed the oracle code in bench/simulate_oracle.py:87-91 and confirmed the finding. The _cycle_keys function returns only frozenset(frozenset(c.modules) for c in cd.added/resolved), completely ignoring c.edges. The Cycle class (src/archy/cycles.py:17-21) does have both modules and edges fields, containing CycleEdge objects with source, target, and lines metadata. These edges ARE reported to users in CLI output (src/archy/cli.py:1357, 1738) and JSON (src/archy/diff.py:196). The oracle's _matches function (line 118) compares only _cycle_keys between sim.cycles and real.cycles, which means two CycleSetDiff objects with identical module sets but different edge details would pass undetected. However, I also reviewed the SPEC_SIMULATE.md (line 82-97) which explicitly states that cycle identity should be based only on frozenset(modules), making this implementation consistent with the documented design. The spec even documents that lines=() is "safe and load-bearing for the validation oracle" because "cycle identity is frozenset(modules)." That said, this creates a gap between what the spec says at line 211 (assert sim.cycles == real.cycles, implying full equality) and what the oracle actually checks (module-set equality only). A bug that produces a cycle with correct modules but incorrect edges (wrong source/target pairs or wrong line numbers within the cycle) would indeed pass undetected.
findings.ticket_notes: This is a real gap in the oracle's validation, but with limited practical impact. The finding correctly identifies that _cycle_keys ignores c.edges. However: (1) The implementation is consistent with the design intent stated in simulate.py lines 14-18 and SPEC_SIMULATE.md lines 82-97, which explicitly document that "cycle identity is frozenset(modules)"; (2) A bug would have to specifically affect cycle-edge computation (not general edge computation), because SCC detection is deterministic - if the same modules form an SCC in both graphs, the internal edges should be the same; (3) The synthetic edge with lines=() affects only line metadata, not edge existence/direction. That said, to align the oracle with the spec's stated comparison "assert sim.cycles == real.cycles" (SPEC line 211) and to catch any edge-level bugs, the oracle should be expanded to also compare the (source, target) pairs from c.edges, as suggested. This would be a defensive improvement, not a critical bug fix. Ticket should specify: (a) expand _cycle_keys to compare edge pairs (source, target), optionally including line numbers for maximum coverage; (b) update the design-intent comment in simulate.py if this becomes more comprehensive; (c) confirm this matches the spec's intent at line 211.

findings.title: SdpViolation instability values not compared
findings.claim: The oracle only compares (source, target) pairs for SDP violations but ignores source_instability and target_instability values. A bug in how simulate computes instability when edges are added would pass silently.
findings.evidence: _sdp_keys returns only frozenset((v.source, v.target) for v in sd.added/resolved), completely excluding v.source_instability and v.target_instability. These are critical fields that get computed in find_sdp_violations (src/archy/layers.py:218-222) using compute_instability(). When an edge is added, node instability values change (I = Ce/(Ce+Ca), where Ce and Ca change with new edges), which can alter which violations are reported and at what magnitude.
findings.impact: If simulate incorrectly computes instability for the hypothetical graph, or if there's an off-by-one error in instability calculation, the oracle would still report 100% pass rate because it only checks the source/target edges, not the computed instability values. The bench results show 0 bug failures, but instability bugs could hide.
findings.suggested_action: Expand _sdp_keys to compare instability values: include v.source_instability and v.target_instability in the comparison with a reasonable epsilon for floating-point equality (similar to the propagation_cost check on line 123-124).
findings.verifier_reasoning: The finding's technical claim is accurate: _sdp_keys (lines 101-105) extracts only (source, target) tuples from SdpViolation objects, completely excluding source_instability and target_instability values. The oracle uses _sdp_keys for comparison on line 120, whereas the unit test in test_simulate.py uses full object equality (line 181). However, the practical risk is limited because: (1) The bench corpus has no archy.yaml configurations, so sdp_violations is always empty tuples in real-repo tests, making the oracle comparison always trivially pass. (2) Both simulate and diff use the identical find_sdp_violations() function from layers.py, so they compute instability values the same way on the same graph structure - any instability bug would affect both equally. The only real scenario where this matters is if SDP were enabled in a future benchmark and there was a bug in simulate's graph construction that wasn't caught elsewhere. The layer-violation smoke test only covers forbid rules, not SDP rules (no 'sdp: {enabled: true}' in its config). The spec in SPEC_SIMULATE.md §7 requires validating sdp_violations, but the bench has gapped coverage.
findings.ticket_notes: This is not a blocker-level bug but a legitimate coverage gap and defensive programming improvement: (1) **Current scope**: SDP violations are never actually tested in the bench oracle because the corpus carries no archy.yaml, so both simulate and diff always report empty sdp_violations tuples. No bug will hide here today. (2) **Future-proofing**: If SDP becomes enabled in real-repo benchmark scenarios, expand _sdp_keys to include instability values with epsilon comparison (e.g., 1e-12 tolerance) for floating-point equality, matching the pattern on lines 123-124 for propagation_cost. (3) **Consistency**: The unit test (test_simulate.py:181) correctly uses full object comparison `assert sim.sdp_violations == real.sdp_violations`, so the weakness is isolated to the bench's _sdp_keys function, not the code under test. (4) **Related coverage**: The bench's _violation_smoke only tests forbid rules, not SDP rules - add SDP configuration to that smoke test if SDP testing is prioritized. Document in the Gaps section that SDP violations lack real-repo oracle coverage due to missing archy.yaml configs in the corpus.

findings.title: Misleading comment in simulate.py about field safety
findings.claim: The comment states that synthetic edges with lines=() are safe because 'none of those read lines', but this conflates 'not needed for graph structure' with 'not part of the data model'. The oracle only checks a subset of fields, not all fields that exist in the data model.
findings.evidence: The comment says 'the simulated and real graphs agree on every field the report compares', which is tautological and misleading. It should clarify that only specific fields (module sets, rule identities) are used for structural computation, not that all fields match. The Cycle, Violation, and SdpViolation objects all have lines fields that WILL differ between simulated and real graphs, and the oracle currently doesn't check them.
findings.impact: Future developers might assume the oracle validates all fields and not realize that lines metadata and instability values are unchecked. This could lead to latent bugs not being caught.
findings.suggested_action: Clarify the comment to explicitly state which fields are used for structural identity (modules, rule identity, source/target pairs) and note that lines and instability are not currently validated by the oracle. Add a TODO or FIXME noting the gap.
findings.verifier_reasoning: The finding is confirmed by code inspection and bench analysis. The oracle validation uses _cycle_keys(), _violation_keys(), and _sdp_keys() which extract only identity tuples (frozenset(modules) for cycles, (from_layer, to_layer, source, target) for violations, (source, target) for SDP violations). These identity functions explicitly exclude the `lines` field that exists in all three data models. The bench results (315/315 matches) validate structural identities only, not metadata fidelity. The unit test (test_oracle_add_matches_real_edit) uses full object equality but only tests scenarios where no cycles form, so the edge-lines discrepancy never actually appears in the tested cases. I verified: (1) CycleEdge, Violation, and SdpViolation all have lines fields (cycles.py:14, layers.py:73, layers.py:89), (2) find_cycles reads lines from the graph (cycles.py:54), (3) synthetic edges have lines=() while real edges have lines=(N,) populated from source files (graph.py:511, graph.py:540), and (4) the bench's _matches() function explicitly uses key-extracting functions that omit lines fields (bench/simulate_oracle.py:118-120).
findings.ticket_notes: The finding is factually correct but the impact is LIMITED to documentation clarity rather than a functional bug. The lines metadata difference does not affect structural predictions because: (1) The oracle validates only the structural identities (cycles' module sets, violations' rule+endpoints, SDP violations' source+target pairs), which match perfectly (315/315 in bench). (2) Score deltas, cycle presence, violation presence, and back-edge predictions are all correct despite lines differences. (3) Lines are informational metadata telling where imports exist in code, not data used in structural computation. The comment in simulate.py:14-18 should be improved to explicitly state: "Cycle identity uses frozenset(modules); violation identity uses (from_layer, to_layer, source, target); SDP violation identity uses (source, target). None of these identity functions use the lines field. The lines metadata will differ between simulated (empty) and real (populated) graphs but do not affect structural predictions because lines are not inputs to cycle detection, violation matching, or score computation. The oracle validates structural identity, not metadata completeness." Additionally, a note could be added that instability values in SdpViolation are also not currently validated by the oracle. This is a documentation gap, not a logic bug in the oracle itself.

findings.title: No validation of SDP violation detection itself when edges are added
findings.location: bench/simulate_oracle.py:199-261, evaluate function and corpus setup
findings.claim: The corpus contains no archy.yaml files with layer rules, and SDP checking is off by default (sdp.enabled=False). This means SDP violations are never actually tested on real repos, only on synthetic 400-node graphs in _violation_smoke. The oracle could pass 100% even if simulate has bugs in SDP violation detection.
findings.evidence: The docs at the end of simulate_oracle_results.md state: 'Violation prediction reuses archy's own find_violations on the hypothetical graph; covered by the synthetic smoke above and unit tests, not by real-repo layer rules (the corpus carries no archy.yaml).' The _violation_smoke function (line 327-354) creates a synthetic graph with specific layers and only checks that forbidden edges are flagged and allowed edges are silent. It does not check instability computation or any interaction with real SDP violations.
findings.impact: Any bug in SDP violation handling (instability computation, edge-attribution, filtering logic) could exist without being caught by the real-corpus tests. The oracle reports 0 bugs, but this only validates the 4 real repos where SDP is disabled. The _violation_smoke is a thin smoke test that does not exercise the full SDP machinery.
findings.suggested_action: Either (1) enable SDP checking in the synthetic test to validate instability computation end-to-end, or (2) add a synthetic corpus that exercises SDP violations and verifies instability values match between simulate and real diff. The current setup tests only boolean presence/absence of violations, not their properties.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I verified the code at the cited locations (/Users/hosanglee/archy/bench/simulate_oracle.py:199-261, simulate_oracle_results.md). The finding is factually accurate:

1. No archy.yaml files exist in bench/replay_cache/ (confirmed by find).
2. In evaluate() line 206, take_snapshot() is called WITHOUT config_path, so config=None, causing lines 119-123 of diff.py to skip SDP violation computation. Both baseline and current snapshots have empty sdp_violations tuples.
3. _violation_smoke (lines 327-354) tests layer-rule violations (forbid/allow), NOT SDP violations (which are about Martin's instability). The synthetic archy.yaml has no sdp: section, so sdp.enabled remains False.
4. The _matches() function line 120 checks _sdp_keys(sim.sdp_violations) == _sdp_keys(real.sdp_violations), but this is trivially true on real-corpus tests (both empty).
5. The oracle validates 315 clean samples on cycles/layers/scoring/back-edges but zero real-repo samples for SDP violations - all SDP tests are synthetic and check only presence/absence of layer violations, not instability computation.

The documented gap at simulate_oracle_results.md line 55 explicitly acknowledges this: "Violation prediction reuses archy's own find_violations on the hypothetical graph; covered by the synthetic smoke above and unit tests, not by real-repo layer rules (the corpus carries no archy.yaml)."

This is a bench coverage gap for SDP, not a bug in simulate itself. The oracle correctly validates 7 other dimensions (cycles, layers, score, back-edges, propagation cost, complexity invariance) across 4 real repos.
findings.ticket_notes: The gap is documented in the codebase's own results file. To fix: (1) add an archy.yaml with sdp: {enabled: true} to _violation_smoke, (2) verify instability computation in both simulate and real diff paths match on test graphs with actual SDP violations (not just presence/absence). This is a bench enhancement, not a correctness bug in simulate.py itself. The oracle still validates the other 7 dimensions comprehensively on 4 real repos with 327 samples (315 clean, 0 mismatches). SDP is out-of-scope for the current oracle but acknowledged as a gap.

gaps.area: Cross-module data-corruption chain: parser/graph resolution -> external classification -> ALL internal-only metrics
gaps.why_underexamined: Every reviewer worked one unit at a time. The confirmed major in code/graph+parser (relative-import resolution returns bare module names for escaped-package imports) was scored only as a parser correctness bug. But instability.py, reach.py (propagation_cost), risk.py, score.py (equality, modularity, acyclicity, depth), affected.py, and hotspots.py ALL filter on the node `external` flag set at graph.py:124/137/158. A misresolved import that lands a node as external (or as a phantom bare-name internal node) silently shifts Ce/Ca counts, ancestor sets, fan-in denominators, the Gini out-degree vector, and the community partition. The result is a wrong overall score and a wrong diff, with NO error and NO finding anywhere connecting resolution accuracy to metric output. This is the single highest-leverage blind spot: a quiet upstream bug poisons every downstream number the tool exists to produce.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Construct a fixture package that triggers the bare-module-name escaped-package resolution path, then assert on the resulting instability map, propagation_cost, edit_risk, and full Score. Diff metrics computed before vs after the resolution fix to quantify how far one resolution error moves overall. Specifically check whether a misresolved node inflates the internal-node set (changing N_internal denominators in risk.py:57 and reach.py) or gets dropped to external (vanishing from every map).

gaps.why_underexamined: risk.py received ZERO findings this round despite being structurally identical to the diff_summary defect that WAS flagged twice as major ('Resolved-cycle risk can be zero when any member hits zero on one factor'). edit_risk = (prop * fan_in * instability)**(1/3) goes to exactly 0 whenever instability=0. A maximally load-bearing sink that the entire project imports (high prop, high fan_in) but that imports nothing internal (instability=0) scores risk=0 and vanishes from archy_high_risk_modules AND from refactor priorities (refactor.py:166 gates on risk>=min_risk). test_risk.py:30-43 enshrines this as correct ('stable sink has zero risk') citing SDP, but never tests the failure mode: the most dangerous module in many real codebases (a central config/types/base module) is exactly a stable sink, and the tool reports it as zero-risk. The docstring rationalizes this; nobody adversarially tested whether the rationalization holds on real corpus modules.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Run compute_edit_risk on the bench corpus and list which modules score exactly 0.0; check by hand whether any are obviously high-blast-radius (base/types/config). Quantify how often instability=0 zeroes out an otherwise top-quartile prop*fan_in module. This is the same theater class as the diff_summary findings but in the live agent-facing tool, not just the diff summarizer.

gaps.area: hotspots.py + refactor.py (v0.30.0, merged #159 one commit before this round) git_churn rename/path-resolution correctness
gaps.why_underexamined: refactor.py is the newest module (the fusion feature) and got NO findings; hotspots got only bench-level findings, none on the code. git_churn (hotspots.py:86-92) reads historical paths from `git log --name-only` and does `(repo_root / rel).resolve()`, then compute_hotspots matches against current node `path` via `str(Path(path).resolve())`. For any file that was renamed/moved across history, the historical path string never matches the current node path, so churn is silently undercounted for exactly the files that moved most (often the highest-churn files). No finding addresses git-follow/rename handling. Separately, refactor.py:173 computes max_hotspot from `hotspots` but max_risk from `candidates` (refactor.py:174) - asymmetric normalization bases that could distort the blend, unexamined.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Create a git fixture that renames a .py file mid-history and assert churn aggregates pre+post-rename commits (it almost certainly will not). Probe whether git log --follow or a rename-aware accumulation is needed. Separately audit the norm_h vs norm_r denominator asymmetry in refactor.py for ranking distortion when the hotspot and risk candidate sets differ in size.

gaps.area: score.py geomean axis-sensitivity (depth 'barely moves overall' asserted, never measured)
gaps.why_underexamined: Two findings (SCORING-methodology 'Depth axis barely moves overall' and 'depth /8 magic number') name the symptom but no reviewer numerically perturbed the geomean. overall = (mod*acy*dep*eq*cpx)**0.2 means each axis's marginal influence depends on the OTHER axes' values (a low axis dominates the partial derivative). The claim 'depth barely moves overall' is only true near depth=1; near depth=0 it dominates. Nobody computed d(overall)/d(axis) across the corpus to show which axis actually drives ranking. Also compute_depth uses condensation longest-path so a single deep chain in one corner sets the whole project's depth axis - a god-chain sensitivity untested.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Numerically sweep each axis 0->1 holding others at corpus-median and plot overall sensitivity; verify the 'barely moves' and 'dominates' claims empirically rather than rhetorically. Test compute_depth on a graph with one long tail vs broad-shallow to confirm longest-path is the intended depth semantics.

gaps.area: affected.py / impact.py glob and depth semantics (affected got a code-finding but the glob translator and disjointness invariant did not)
gaps.why_underexamined: code/cli flagged affected depth validation, but affected.py's own _compile_glob (lines 170-207) reimplements recursive-glob-to-regex and is shared by the test classifier; the layers/contracts review already found a `**`-not-preceded-by-dot regex bug in a DIFFERENT pattern translator (layers.py), strongly suggesting the same bug class lives here untested. _compile_glob handles `**/` and trailing `**` but a bare `**` mid-pattern not followed by `/` falls into the `.*` branch which crosses `/` boundaries - possibly matching unintended segments. The docstring invariant 'impacted_tests and impacted_modules are disjoint by construction' is asserted but the classifier runs path.resolve().relative_to(root) which silently returns False (non-test) for any node outside root, quietly misclassifying out-of-root nodes as modules.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Unit-test _compile_glob against patterns like `a/**b`, `**`, `**.py`, and segment-crossing cases; compare to the layers.py `**` bug to see if the same defect recurs. Test the disjointness invariant with a node whose path is outside project_root (symlinked/vendored) to see if it lands in impacted_modules wrongly.

gaps.area: Determinism / stability of networkx greedy community detection feeding modularity (and call-weighted Q)
gaps.why_underexamined: compute_modularity and compute_modularity_weighted both call nx.community.greedy_modularity_communities, whose output partition can be order-sensitive / non-unique on ties. No finding anywhere checks run-to-run determinism of raw_q, community_count, or the weighted-vs-unweighted GAP that CALL_WEIGHTED_Q calls 'the load-bearing signal'. If the partition is unstable, the gap (the entire justification for the call-weighted diagnostic) is noise. The bench findings questioned the gap's meaning but not its reproducibility.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Run compute_score N times on a fixed mid-size corpus graph and check whether raw_modularity, community_count, and the weighted/unweighted Q gap are bit-identical; permute node insertion order and re-run. If the gap varies across runs, the call-weighted Q diagnostic is measuring partition instability, not call traffic.

gaps.area: Research claims still entirely unaudited: propagation_cost defect-prediction citations and MacCormack/Lakos NCCD equivalence
gaps.why_underexamined: reach.py's docstring makes strong empirical claims ('most-validated single architectural metric', 'multiple Spearman-significant studies', MacCormack-Rusnak-Baldwin 2006, 'replicated in 2026 ATD literature', NCCD 'same metric family different normalization'). RESEARCH_METRICS+synthesis findings audited HN-sourced and Substack-sourced claims and dead links, but did NOT audit the propagation-cost literature claims that are the foundation of risk.py, refactor.py, and the propagation_cost diagnostic. The NCCD r=0.000 'orthogonal' finding contradicts the docstring's 'same metric family' claim - an unresolved internal inconsistency.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Verify the MacCormack 2006 propagation-cost-to-defect Spearman claim against the actual paper and check whether the cited 2026 replication exists. Reconcile reach.py's 'NCCD same metric family' with the synthesis finding of r=0.000 vs depth - if NCCD really is the same family, the zero correlation is a measurement bug, not orthogonality.

gaps.area: Bench corpus assumption: 27 pinned projects, all stable, none mid-refactor, used to validate a tool whose entire pitch is the agent edit loop
gaps.why_underexamined: corpus findings noted self-reference and selection bias, but the deeper untested assumption is temporal: every benchmark scores a single frozen snapshot, while archy's value claim (simulate, diff, edit-risk, refactor-next) is about DELTAS during active editing. inloop_prevalence is the only delta study and its findings show the corpus is too small (N=5 events) and skewed. No bench ever validated that archy's metrics MOVE CORRECTLY when code is edited - only that they have plausible cross-sectional distributions. The whole adversarial round measured static correctness; the dynamic correctness that the product sells is essentially unmeasured.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Build a delta-validation bench: take real refactor PRs (cycle-breaking, god-module splits) and verify archy's before/after scores move in the expected direction with expected magnitude. This is the missing falsification gate the corpus finding named but no one built.

gaps.area: Suspiciously thin: trend.py, history.py float/int and JSONL findings exist but no cross-version schema-migration integration test against real on-disk history
gaps.why_underexamined: history/trend got several findings (strict int rejecting floats, missing pre-v0.7 row coverage, no timestamp validation) but these were spotted by reading, not by replaying a real multi-version JSONL file. index+watcher findings flagged 'no schema version bump protection for ParseResult' and 'deserialization error crashes sync' - the same forward/backward-compat risk exists for the history JSONL but was treated as a separate, lesser concern. The interaction (an old cache + new ParseResult schema + old history rows in one session) was never exercised end to end.
gaps.what_to_probe_next: Generate a JSONL with rows from v0.6, v0.7, v0.20, v0.30 schemas plus a stale ParseResult cache, then run trend + sync in one process and confirm graceful handling rather than per-row reading-it-looks-fine. Add an explicit schema-version field check shared between index cache and history.

completeness.confidence_reasoning: The per-unit coverage this round is genuinely broad and deep: nearly every source module and bench has multiple confirmed findings, and the findings are specific and credible. That raises confidence on STATIC, single-unit correctness to high. But three structural blind spots keep overall confidence at medium, not high. (1) Cross-module data-flow was almost entirely unexamined: the resolution -> external-classification -> all-metrics chain means a confirmed parser bug can silently corrupt every output, and no finding connects these layers. (2) Two whole modules central to the agent-facing value proposition got essentially no code findings (risk.py: zero; refactor.py: zero) despite risk.py containing the same geometric-mean-zero defect class that was flagged as major elsewhere - that asymmetry signals the review was unit-myopic, not that those modules are clean. (3) The dynamic/delta correctness that the product actually sells (edit-loop, simulate, diff, refactor-next) is validated only by one small (N=5) study; the corpus is all static snapshots. Until someone tests that metrics move correctly under real edits and that one resolution error does not poison the score/diff, 'archy is well-understood' is unproven. I have medium confidence the round found most local bugs and low-to-medium confidence it found the load-bearing systemic ones.
